subtopics.title: T2 Bonding and Structure · WS 2.2; WS 3.7

questions.question: Classify carbon dioxide as ionic or covalent. Explain your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide is covalent. Carbon and oxygen are non-metals. They share electrons to form covalent bonds.
markingPoints: Carbon dioxide is covalent. Carbon and oxygen are non-metals. They share electrons to form covalent bonds.

questions.question: Classify magnesium oxide as ionic or covalent. Explain your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium oxide is ionic. Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal. Electrons are transferred from magnesium to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions.
markingPoints: Magnesium oxide is ionic. Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal. Electrons are transferred from magnesium to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions.

questions.question: Describe the structure of carbon nanotubes and give one use.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon nanotubes are long hollow cylinders of carbon atoms. They have a high length-to-diameter ratio and can conduct electricity. They are used in electronics or as reinforcing materials.
markingPoints: Carbon nanotubes are long hollow cylinders of carbon atoms. They have a high length-to-diameter ratio and can conduct electricity. They are used in electronics or as reinforcing materials.

questions.question: Describe the structure of fullerenes and give one use.
questions.modelAnswer: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms arranged in hollow cages or tubes. One use is drug delivery, lubricants or reinforcing materials.
markingPoints: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms arranged in hollow cages or tubes. One use is drug delivery, lubricants or reinforcing materials.

questions.question: Hydrogen chloride is covalent, but hydrochloric acid solution conducts electricity. Explain both statements.
questions.modelAnswer:
In hydrogen chloride molecules, hydrogen and chlorine share electrons, so the bonding is covalent.
Pure hydrogen chloride consists of neutral molecules and does not conduct.
When dissolved in water, it forms mobile H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
These ions carry charge through the solution.
markingPoints: In hydrogen chloride molecules, hydrogen and chlorine share electrons, so the bonding is covalent.
Pure hydrogen chloride consists of neutral molecules and does not conduct.
When dissolved in water, it forms mobile H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
These ions carry charge through the solution.

questions.question: Use group number to state the charges of sodium, magnesium, oxygen and chlorine ions. Then write the formula of magnesium oxide.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sodium forms Na⁺; magnesium forms Mg²⁺; oxygen forms O²⁻; chlorine forms Cl⁻.
Magnesium oxide is MgO because one Mg²⁺ balances one O²⁻, giving no overall charge.
markingPoints: Sodium forms Na⁺; magnesium forms Mg²⁺; oxygen forms O²⁻; chlorine forms Cl⁻.
Magnesium oxide is MgO because one Mg²⁺ balances one O²⁻, giving no overall charge.

questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for sodium oxide, Na₂O. Show only outer-shell electrons, brackets and ion charges.
questions.modelAnswer:
Two Na atoms each transfer one outer electron to O.
Diagram shows [Na]⁺, [O]²⁻, [Na]⁺ in brackets with charges.
Oxide has a complete outer shell of eight electrons, including one electron from each sodium.
markingPoints: Two Na atoms each transfer one outer electron to O.
Diagram shows [Na]⁺, [O]²⁻, [Na]⁺ in brackets with charges.
Oxide has a complete outer shell of eight electrons, including one electron from each sodium.

questions.question: Explain fully how magnesium and chlorine form magnesium chloride, MgCl₂. Include electron transfer, ion charges and electrostatic attraction.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺.
Each of two chlorine atoms (2,8,7) gains one electron to form two Cl⁻ ions.
Oppositely charged ions attract strongly in all directions by electrostatic forces, forming a giant ionic lattice.
Chemical formula MgCl₂ balances charge.
markingPoints: Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺.
Each of two chlorine atoms (2,8,7) gains one electron to form two Cl⁻ ions.
Oppositely charged ions attract strongly in all directions by electrostatic forces, forming a giant ionic lattice.
Chemical formula MgCl₂ balances charge.

questions.question: Aluminium conducts electricity better than sodium. Explain this using metallic bonding.
questions.modelAnswer: Both metals have delocalised electrons. Each aluminium atom provides three delocalised electrons, whereas each sodium atom provides one. More delocalised electrons are available to carry charge in aluminium.
markingPoints: Both metals have delocalised electrons. Each aluminium atom provides three delocalised electrons, whereas each sodium atom provides one. More delocalised electrons are available to carry charge in aluminium.

questions.question: Explain why a wire made from a pure metal usually conducts electricity better than a wire made from an alloy.
questions.modelAnswer: Both contain delocalised electrons that carry charge. In an alloy, different-sized atoms distort the regular layers. This makes it harder for the delocalised electrons to move through the structure, so the alloy has lower electrical conductivity.
markingPoints: Both contain delocalised electrons that carry charge. In an alloy, different-sized atoms distort the regular layers. This makes it harder for the delocalised electrons to move through the structure, so the alloy has lower electrical conductivity.

questions.question: Determine the formulae of aluminium oxide, calcium chloride and magnesium nitride from Al³⁺, O²⁻, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻, Mg²⁺ and N³⁻. Explain the rule used.
questions.modelAnswer:
Al₂O₃, CaCl₂, Mg₃N₂.
Total positive charge must equal total negative charge so the compound is electrically neutral.
Use the smallest whole-number ratio of ions.
markingPoints: Al₂O₃, CaCl₂, Mg₃N₂.
Total positive charge must equal total negative charge so the compound is electrically neutral.
Use the smallest whole-number ratio of ions.

questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for H₂.
questions.modelAnswer: Show one shared pair of electrons between two hydrogen atoms.
markingPoints: Show one shared pair of electrons between two hydrogen atoms.

questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for CH₄.
questions.modelAnswer: Show four shared pairs between the carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms.
markingPoints: Show four shared pairs between the carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms.

questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for H₂O.
questions.modelAnswer: Show two shared pairs between oxygen and two hydrogen atoms, with two lone pairs on oxygen.
markingPoints: Show two shared pairs between oxygen and two hydrogen atoms, with two lone pairs on oxygen.

questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for HCl.
questions.modelAnswer: Show one shared pair between H and Cl and three lone pairs on the chlorine atom.
markingPoints: Show one shared pair between H and Cl and three lone pairs on the chlorine atom.

questions.question: Explain what a covalent bond is.
questions.modelAnswer: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. There is electrostatic attraction between the shared electrons and both nuclei.
markingPoints: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. There is electrostatic attraction between the shared electrons and both nuclei.

questions.question: A molecule contains two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms. Write its molecular formula and state why this does not show its structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
N₂O₄.
A molecular formula gives only numbers/types of atoms, not their arrangement or which atoms are bonded.
markingPoints: N₂O₄.
A molecular formula gives only numbers/types of atoms, not their arrangement or which atoms are bonded.

questions.question: A substance has a melting point of −15 °C and a boiling point of 75 °C. State whether it is solid, liquid or gas at −20 °C, 25 °C and 90 °C. Explain your answers.
questions.modelAnswer:
At −20 °C it is a solid because the temperature is below its melting point.
At 25 °C it is a liquid because the temperature is above its melting point but below its boiling point.
At 90 °C it is a gas because the temperature is above its boiling point.
markingPoints: At −20 °C it is a solid because the temperature is below its melting point.
At 25 °C it is a liquid because the temperature is above its melting point but below its boiling point.
At 90 °C it is a gas because the temperature is above its boiling point.

questions.question: Compare the arrangement, movement and energy of particles in a solid, liquid and gas. Explain changes of state.
questions.modelAnswer:
Solid: close, regular, vibrate about fixed positions.
Liquid: close, irregular, move past each other.
Gas: far apart, rapid random motion.
Heating transfers energy to particles.
At melting/boiling energy overcomes attractions without changing chemical identity.
Cooling reverses the changes.
Mass is conserved.
markingPoints: Solid: close, regular, vibrate about fixed positions.
Liquid: close, irregular, move past each other.
Gas: far apart, rapid random motion.
Heating transfers energy to particles.
At melting/boiling energy overcomes attractions without changing chemical identity.
Cooling reverses the changes.
Mass is conserved.

questions.question: State what each state symbol means: (s), (l), (g) and (aq).
questions.modelAnswer: (s) solid; (l) liquid; (g) gas; (aq) dissolved in water (aqueous).
markingPoints: (s) solid; (l) liquid; (g) gas; (aq) dissolved in water (aqueous).

questions.question: Use metallic bonding to explain why metals are malleable.
questions.modelAnswer: Layers of metal ions can slide past each other while the attraction to delocalised electrons is maintained.
markingPoints: Layers of metal ions can slide past each other while the attraction to delocalised electrons is maintained.

questions.question: Use metallic bonding to explain why metals conduct electricity and heat.
questions.modelAnswer: Delocalised electrons move through the structure. They carry electrical charge and transfer energy.
markingPoints: Delocalised electrons move through the structure. They carry electrical charge and transfer energy.

questions.question: Use metallic bonding to explain why metals have high melting points.
questions.modelAnswer: Strong electrostatic attractions between positive ions and delocalised electrons need a lot of energy to overcome.
markingPoints: Strong electrostatic attractions between positive ions and delocalised electrons need a lot of energy to overcome.

questions.question: Describe metallic bonding.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals contain a giant structure of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalised electrons. Strong electrostatic attraction acts between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
markingPoints: Metals contain a giant structure of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalised electrons. Strong electrostatic attraction acts between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.

questions.question: A ball-and-stick model shows atoms far apart connected by sticks. Give two ways it can misrepresent a real solid.
questions.modelAnswer:
Atoms/electron clouds are not separated by large empty gaps at the model scale.
Sticks are not literal bonds.
Atom sizes/bond lengths may not be to scale.
Model does not show electron density or movement.
Any two explained.
markingPoints: Atoms/electron clouds are not separated by large empty gaps at the model scale.
Sticks are not literal bonds.
Atom sizes/bond lengths may not be to scale.
Model does not show electron density or movement.
Any two explained.

questions.question: Explain why an ionic solid is brittle when struck, whereas a pure metal can be bent into shape.
questions.modelAnswer:
In an ionic lattice, a force can shift layers so that ions with the same charge become next to each other.
Like charges repel, so the lattice splits.
In a pure metal, layers of atoms can slide past each other while metallic bonding is maintained by delocalised electrons, so the metal can bend.
markingPoints: In an ionic lattice, a force can shift layers so that ions with the same charge become next to each other.
Like charges repel, so the lattice splits.
In a pure metal, layers of atoms can slide past each other while metallic bonding is maintained by delocalised electrons, so the metal can bend.

questions.question: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
questions.modelAnswer:
In the solid, ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot carry charge through it.
When molten, ions are free to move and carry electrical charge.
markingPoints: In the solid, ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot carry charge through it.
When molten, ions are free to move and carry electrical charge.

questions.question: Explain how conductivity observations provide evidence for the ionic bonding model.
questions.modelAnswer:
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because ions are fixed.
Molten or dissolved ionic compounds conduct because ions can move and carry charge.
The change supports a lattice of charged particles rather than neutral molecules.
markingPoints: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because ions are fixed.
Molten or dissolved ionic compounds conduct because ions can move and carry charge.
The change supports a lattice of charged particles rather than neutral molecules.

questions.question: Explain why sodium chloride does not conduct electricity when solid but conducts when molten or dissolved.
questions.modelAnswer: In solid sodium chloride, the ions are fixed in place and cannot carry charge. When molten or dissolved, ions are free to move and carry charge.
markingPoints: In solid sodium chloride, the ions are fixed in place and cannot carry charge. When molten or dissolved, ions are free to move and carry charge.

questions.question: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice. There are strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions. A lot of energy is needed to overcome these attractions.
markingPoints: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice. There are strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions. A lot of energy is needed to overcome these attractions.

questions.question: Three metals could be used for overhead power cables. Aluminium: conductivity 38 units, density 2.7 g/cm³, £1.50/kg. Copper: 60 units, 9.0 g/cm³, £7.00/kg. Silver: 63 units, 10.5 g/cm³, £640/kg. Choose the most suitable metal and justify your choice using the data.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium is the best overall choice for overhead cables. It conducts less well than copper and silver, but is much lighter and far cheaper. It has sufficient electrical conductivity while reducing the load on supports and the cost. Silver conducts best but is far too expensive; copper conducts better but is heavier and more costly.
markingPoints: Aluminium is the best overall choice for overhead cables. It conducts less well than copper and silver, but is much lighter and far cheaper. It has sufficient electrical conductivity while reducing the load on supports and the cost. Silver conducts best but is far too expensive; copper conducts better but is heavier and more costly.

questions.question: Magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. Suggest why using ion charges.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have greater charges than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, producing stronger electrostatic attractions in the lattice.
More energy is needed to overcome them.
markingPoints: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have greater charges than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, producing stronger electrostatic attractions in the lattice.
More energy is needed to overcome them.

questions.question: Plan a fair test to compare the electrical conductivity of sodium chloride as a solid and when molten or dissolved.
questions.modelAnswer:
Use the same conductivity circuit and electrode spacing.
Test solid sodium chloride and a fixed-concentration solution or molten sample.
Keep potential difference and temperature controlled where appropriate.
Rinse electrodes.
Record current.
Use eye protection and avoid unsafe school melting if unsuitable.
markingPoints: Use the same conductivity circuit and electrode spacing.
Test solid sodium chloride and a fixed-concentration solution or molten sample.
Keep potential difference and temperature controlled where appropriate.
Rinse electrodes.
Record current.
Use eye protection and avoid unsafe school melting if unsuitable.

questions.question: Explain why simple molecular substances do not conduct electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: They have no mobile charged particles.
markingPoints: They have no mobile charged particles.

questions.question: Explain why boiling point generally increases with molecular size.
questions.modelAnswer: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.
markingPoints: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.question: Explain why simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points.
questions.modelAnswer: Weak intermolecular forces between molecules need little energy to overcome.
markingPoints: Weak intermolecular forces between molecules need little energy to overcome.

questions.question: Methane boils at −162 °C and octane at 126 °C. Explain the difference without saying that covalent bonds break.
questions.modelAnswer:
Octane molecules are larger and have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate molecules.
Covalent bonds within molecules remain intact during boiling.
markingPoints: Octane molecules are larger and have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate molecules.
Covalent bonds within molecules remain intact during boiling.

questions.question: Define a monomer and a polymer.
questions.modelAnswer: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to other molecules. A polymer is a large molecule made from many repeating monomer units.
markingPoints: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to other molecules. A polymer is a large molecule made from many repeating monomer units.

questions.question: Define a polymer.
questions.modelAnswer: A very large molecule made from repeating monomer units.
markingPoints: A very large molecule made from repeating monomer units.

questions.question: Explain why many polymers are solids at room temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Intermolecular forces act between long chains. Many contact points make these forces relatively strong.
markingPoints: Intermolecular forces act between long chains. Many contact points make these forces relatively strong.

questions.question: Poly(ethene) is solid at room temperature but ethene is a gas. Explain using structure and forces.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ethene is small/simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces.
Poly(ethene) has long chains and stronger intermolecular attractions across many contact points, so more energy is needed to separate chains.
markingPoints: Ethene is small/simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces.
Poly(ethene) has long chains and stronger intermolecular attractions across many contact points, so more energy is needed to separate chains.

questions.question: A sample has a high melting point and does not conduct electricity as a solid or when molten. Identify the likely structure and give a reason for each property.
questions.modelAnswer:
It is likely a giant covalent structure.
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, giving a high melting point.
There are no mobile ions or delocalised electrons to carry electrical charge, so it does not conduct in either state.
markingPoints: It is likely a giant covalent structure.
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, giving a high melting point.
There are no mobile ions or delocalised electrons to carry electrical charge, so it does not conduct in either state.

questions.question: Explain why giant covalent structures have high melting points.
questions.modelAnswer: Many strong covalent bonds need to be broken.
markingPoints: Many strong covalent bonds need to be broken.

questions.question: Explain why most giant covalent structures do not conduct electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: They have no mobile ions or delocalised electrons.
markingPoints: They have no mobile ions or delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. Explain using bonding and structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each graphite carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move and carry charge.
Each diamond carbon bonds to four others, so all outer electrons are localised in covalent bonds.
markingPoints: Each graphite carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move and carry charge.
Each diamond carbon bonds to four others, so all outer electrons are localised in covalent bonds.

questions.question:
Substance A has mp 801 °C and conducts only when molten.
B has mp −98 °C and never conducts.
C has mp 3550 °C and conducts as a solid; it is soft.
D has mp 1710 °C and never conducts.
Part (a): Identify the most likely structure type of each.
Part (b): Justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
A giant ionic: high mp.
Mobile ions only molten.
B simple molecular: low mp.
No mobile charge.
C graphite/giant covalent layered carbon: very high mp, delocalised electrons, soft layers.
D giant covalent such as SiO₂: very high mp and no mobile charge.
markingPoints: A giant ionic: high mp.
Mobile ions only molten.
B simple molecular: low mp.
No mobile charge.
C graphite/giant covalent layered carbon: very high mp, delocalised electrons, soft layers.
D giant covalent such as SiO₂: very high mp and no mobile charge.

questions.question: Explain why testing only one physical property may be insufficient to identify an unknown bonding type.
questions.modelAnswer:
Different structures can share a property and exceptions exist, such as graphite conducting.
A conclusion based on several independent properties is better supported.
markingPoints: Different structures can share a property and exceptions exist, such as graphite conducting.
A conclusion based on several independent properties is better supported.

questions.question: Design measurements that could distinguish a simple molecular substance from a giant covalent substance.
questions.modelAnswer:
Compare melting point, solubility and electrical conductivity using equal samples and controlled methods.
Simple molecules generally melt at low temperatures.
Giant covalent structures have very high melting points.
Graphite conducts, so several properties are needed rather than one result.
markingPoints: Compare melting point, solubility and electrical conductivity using equal samples and controlled methods.
Simple molecules generally melt at low temperatures.
Giant covalent structures have very high melting points.
Graphite conducts, so several properties are needed rather than one result.

questions.question: Give one use of diamond that follows from its properties.
questions.modelAnswer: Cutting or drilling tools because diamond is hard.
markingPoints: Cutting or drilling tools because diamond is hard.

questions.question: Give one use of graphite that follows from its properties.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrodes because graphite conducts electricity, or lubricants because its layers slide over each other.
markingPoints: Electrodes because graphite conducts electricity, or lubricants because its layers slide over each other.

questions.question: Compare the structures and electrical conductivity of diamond and graphite.
questions.modelAnswer: Both are giant covalent structures. In diamond, each carbon forms four bonds and there are no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon forms three bonds and one electron per carbon is delocalised, so it conducts.
markingPoints: Both are giant covalent structures. In diamond, each carbon forms four bonds and there are no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon forms three bonds and one electron per carbon is delocalised, so it conducts.

questions.question: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: It has no delocalised electrons.
markingPoints: It has no delocalised electrons.

questions.question: Explain why diamond has a high melting point.
questions.modelAnswer: Many strong covalent bonds need lots of energy to break.
markingPoints: Many strong covalent bonds need lots of energy to break.

questions.question: Explain why diamond is hard.
questions.modelAnswer: Each carbon forms four strong covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional structure.
markingPoints: Each carbon forms four strong covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional structure.

questions.question: Explain why graphite has a high melting point.
questions.modelAnswer: Many strong covalent bonds are present in its layers.
markingPoints: Many strong covalent bonds are present in its layers.

questions.question: Explain why graphite conducts electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: Each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move through the layers.
markingPoints: Each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move through the layers.

questions.question: Explain why graphite is soft/slippery.
questions.modelAnswer: Weak forces between layers allow the layers to slide.
markingPoints: Weak forces between layers allow the layers to slide.

questions.question: Compare the properties of thermosetting and thermosoftening polymers in terms of their structures.
questions.modelAnswer:
Thermosofteners have separate chains with weak intermolecular forces, so chains slide when heated and the polymer softens.
Thermosets have strong cross-links between chains, preventing sliding, so they do not soften readily.
markingPoints: Thermosofteners have separate chains with weak intermolecular forces, so chains slide when heated and the polymer softens.
Thermosets have strong cross-links between chains, preventing sliding, so they do not soften readily.

questions.question: Describe graphene and give one reason it is useful.
questions.modelAnswer: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, each bonded to three others. It conducts electricity and is strong, so it can be used in electronics or composite materials.
markingPoints: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, each bonded to three others. It conducts electricity and is strong, so it can be used in electronics or composite materials.

questions.question: Explain why graphene conducts electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: Delocalised electrons move through the sheet.
markingPoints: Delocalised electrons move through the sheet.

questions.question: Describe the structure of graphene.
questions.modelAnswer: A single layer of carbon atoms; each carbon bonds to three others in hexagons.
markingPoints: A single layer of carbon atoms; each carbon bonds to three others in hexagons.

questions.question: Explain why graphene is strong and light.
questions.modelAnswer: Strong covalent bonds make it strong; it is one atom thick, so it is light.
markingPoints: Strong covalent bonds make it strong; it is one atom thick, so it is light.

questions.question: Explain why graphene is both strong and able to conduct electricity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Strong covalent bonds extend across the carbon sheet, giving strength.
Each carbon forms three bonds, leaving delocalised electrons that move across the sheet and carry charge.
markingPoints: Strong covalent bonds extend across the carbon sheet, giving strength.
Each carbon forms three bonds, leaving delocalised electrons that move across the sheet and carry charge.

questions.question: Describe the structures of fullerenes and carbon nanotubes and link them to two uses each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fullerenes are hollow carbon molecules, often cages such as C₆₀.
Uses include drug delivery because molecules can be enclosed, and catalysts/lubricants due to large surface/shape.
Nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes.
High tensile strength suits reinforcement, conductivity suits electronics, and large surface area suits catalysts.
markingPoints: Fullerenes are hollow carbon molecules, often cages such as C₆₀.
Uses include drug delivery because molecules can be enclosed, and catalysts/lubricants due to large surface/shape.
Nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes.
High tensile strength suits reinforcement, conductivity suits electronics, and large surface area suits catalysts.

questions.question: Explain why silicon dioxide does not conduct electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: It has no delocalised electrons or ions that are free to move and carry charge.
markingPoints: It has no delocalised electrons or ions that are free to move and carry charge.

questions.question: Explain why silicon dioxide has a high melting point.
questions.modelAnswer: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, requiring a large amount of energy.
markingPoints: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, requiring a large amount of energy.

questions.question: Explain why silicon dioxide is hard.
questions.modelAnswer: Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice.
markingPoints: Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice.

questions.question: Describe metallic bonding and use it to explain why metals conduct electricity and heat, have high melting points and are malleable.
questions.modelAnswer:
Giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
Strong electrostatic attraction between ions and electrons requires much energy to overcome, which means a higher melting point.
Delocalised electrons are free to  move and transfer charge/thermal energy throughtout the structure.
Layers of ions can slide while attraction to electrons remains, so metals are malleable
markingPoints: Giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
Strong electrostatic attraction between ions and electrons requires much energy to overcome, which means a higher melting point.
Delocalised electrons are free to  move and transfer charge/thermal energy throughtout the structure.
Layers of ions can slide while attraction to electrons remains, so metals are malleable

questions.question:
Substance X conducts as a solid and is malleable.
Y is brittle, has a high melting point and conducts only when molten.
Identify the bonding in X and Y and justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
X metallic: delocalised electrons conduct and layers can slide.
Y ionic: strong lattice gives high melting point.
Ions fixed in solid but mobile when molten.
Brittleness is consistent with shifted like charges repelling.
markingPoints: X metallic: delocalised electrons conduct and layers can slide.
Y ionic: strong lattice gives high melting point.
Ions fixed in solid but mobile when molten.
Brittleness is consistent with shifted like charges repelling.

questions.question: A cube-shaped nanoparticle has side length 5.0 nm. Calculate its surface area, volume and simplest surface area : volume ratio.
questions.modelAnswer:
Surface area = 6 × 5.0² = 150 nm².
Volume = 5.0³ = 125 nm³.
Surface area : volume = 150 : 125 = 6 : 5.
markingPoints: Surface area = 6 × 5.0² = 150 nm².
Volume = 5.0³ = 125 nm³.
Surface area : volume = 150 : 125 = 6 : 5.

questions.question: Explain why pure metals are usually more malleable than alloys and why alloys are often harder.
questions.modelAnswer:
In a pure metal, equal-sized atoms form regular layers that slide.
An alloy contains different-sized atoms that distort the layers and obstruct their movement, so more force is needed and the alloy is harder.
markingPoints: In a pure metal, equal-sized atoms form regular layers that slide.
An alloy contains different-sized atoms that distort the layers and obstruct their movement, so more force is needed and the alloy is harder.

questions.question: A nanoparticle cube has side 10 nm and a larger cube has side 1 μm. Explain why the nanoparticle has a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio.
questions.modelAnswer:
Surface area scales with length squared while volume scales with length cubed.
As size decreases, volume falls faster than surface area, so surface area per unit volume increases.
markingPoints: Surface area scales with length squared while volume scales with length cubed.
As size decreases, volume falls faster than surface area, so surface area per unit volume increases.

questions.question: Evaluate the use of nanoparticles when evidence about long-term health effects is incomplete.
questions.modelAnswer:
Balance benefits such as high surface-area applications against uncertain toxicity and environmental persistence.
Consider dose, exposure route and particle size.
Use controlled studies and regulation.
A qualified conclusion is justified rather than claiming they are safe or unsafe in all uses.
markingPoints: Balance benefits such as high surface-area applications against uncertain toxicity and environmental persistence.
Consider dose, exposure route and particle size.
Use controlled studies and regulation.
A qualified conclusion is justified rather than claiming they are safe or unsafe in all uses.

questions.question:
A particle has diameter 4.0 × 10⁻⁸ m.
Convert this to nanometres and classify it as a nanoparticle, fine particle or coarse particle.
State the usual nanoparticle size range.
questions.modelAnswer:
4.0 × 10⁻⁸ m × 10⁹ nm/m = 40 nm.
It is a nanoparticle.
Nanoparticles are approximately 1–100 nm in diameter.
markingPoints: It is a nanoparticle.
Nanoparticles are approximately 1–100 nm in diameter.

questions.question: Explain why nanoparticles can be more effective catalysts than the same mass of larger particles and why only a small mass may be needed.
questions.modelAnswer:
Smaller particles have a much larger surface-area-to-volume ratio.
For the same mass, more atoms are exposed at the surface, providing more active sites and increasing collision frequency/rate.
Therefore a smaller mass can give the required effect.
markingPoints: Smaller particles have a much larger surface-area-to-volume ratio.
For the same mass, more atoms are exposed at the surface, providing more active sites and increasing collision frequency/rate.
Therefore a smaller mass can give the required effect.

questions.question:
A sunscreen containing nanoparticles is transparent and blocks UV.
